subtype: Approach: thinking before posting with a simple test [Thinking]
passage:
Wednesday, 10:30 pm.
Typed a long angry post about how Sharmila's half of our group project came in a day late again. It felt AMAZING to type. Thumb over Post. Then I remembered my own test: would I be fine if Mrs Kapoor, Papa and someone hiring me ten years from now all read this? Teacher: no. Papa: definitely not, he'd ask why I didn't just talk to her. Future boss: probably decides I'm someone who trashes teammates. I deleted the draft and texted Sharmila instead: “Can we put dates next to each task?” Amma says her boy has a temper. Tonight the temper stayed in my notes app, and nobody saw the ugly version. Test passed. I'm using it again.
— Rehan

qa.q: Who does Rehan imagine reading his post?
qa.a: Rehan imagines Mrs Kapoor, Papa and someone hiring him ten years from now.

qa.q: What was Rehan feeling when he typed the angry post?
qa.a: Rehan was angry, and venting felt amazing, until his own test made him uneasy.

qa.q: What else could Rehan try about the late work?
qa.a: Rehan could talk to Sharmila and, if needed, the teacher about clear dates, which he began by texting about dates for each task.

qa.q: How might Sharmila see the text about dates?
qa.a: Sharmila may find it reasonable and much less hurtful than a public rant, so she can fix the delay without being shamed.

grounding: A student asks whether a teacher, a parent and a future employer would be fine with the post and keeps an angry rant off the internet.

subtype: Approach: thinking before posting with a simple test [Thinking]
passage:
In their town of Nagaur, the school bus had broken down for the third time that month, and Gautam had walked four kilometres in the heat. That evening, on the family phone, he typed a long post: the bus contractor was a thief, the principal didn't care, the whole school was a joke.
His thumb hovered over the button. Then he remembered what his cousin Parveen had taught him: before you post anything, picture three people reading it. A teacher. Ammi. Someone who might hire you one day.
He pictured Sharma Sir reading “the whole school is a joke”. His face went warm. He pictured Ammi, who knew the contractor's wife from the mandir. Then a stranger in an office years from now, scrolling.
He deleted the post. Instead, with two other students, he wrote a short, polite letter about the bus, and they gave it to Sharma Sir the next morning.

qa.q: How far did Gautam walk in the heat?
What was Gautam feeling as he typed the post?
qa.a: Gautam was angry and exhausted after the long walk, frustrated at the third breakdown.

qa.q: Why was the polite letter a better choice than the post?
qa.a: It raised the real problem with someone who could act, without words he'd regret teachers, family or employers seeing.

qa.q: How might Sharma Sir have reacted to the post, compared with the letter?
qa.a: The post would likely have hurt and angered him; the letter lets him take the complaint seriously.

grounding: Shows a student picturing a teacher, a parent and a future employer reading an angry post, deleting it, and raising the complaint properly instead.
